l: Sixth Lecture, Called the Cleaning, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The Sixth Lecture teaches religious discipline, renunciation, endurance, non-injury, and liberation while warning against worldliness, lust, sinfulness, and attachment.

l: great heroes, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The great heroes preach wisdom and liberation, endure mendicant hardships, instruct disciples, and achieve victory through right faith and control.

l: parents, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Parents lament and cry when their children leave the world for the glorious road, urging them not to leave; the ascetic, consulting pleasure and passions, does not take refuge in family.

l: disciples, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Disciples are regularly instructed day and night by knowledge-endowed great heroes, receiving knowledge as birds feed their young.

l: teacher, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: instructs disciples [regularly day and night] The teacher is spoken to harshly by men who neglect abstract meditation and religious instruction. Some dispute the teacher's authority or call virtuous religious men worthless.

l: doctrine of renunciation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_proclaimed renunciation [by the speaker] The doctrine of renunciation is proclaimed for those who seek release from the dangers of disease, attachment, and worldliness. It requires attentiveness, non-injury, and the abandonment of worldly desires.

l: effects of works, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: A sage who is well instructed in the law and leads a life of abstinence is a destroyer of the effects of works. One who destroys them successively gives up sinfulness.

l: worldliness, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: causes destruction [through attachment and lust] Worldliness is associated with attachment, sensuality, and the failure to persevere in religious life. Those who quit worldliness should bear disagreeable feelings while maintaining the right view.

l: hardships of a mendicant's life, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The hardships of a mendicant's life include abuse, blows, injury, reproaches, hunger, cold, heat, grass, gnats, mosquitoes, and other troubles. A hero and a religious mendicant should bear them patiently.

l: meditation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Asceticism is shown through fasting, thirst, exposure to heat and cold, silence, meditation, and refusal of bodily comforts. Mahâvîra abandoned care of the body and endured hardships without resentment or desire.

l: right faith, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: causes victory [for the learned, wise, and steadfast hero] Right faith enables the learned, wise, and steadfast hero to remain victorious. It supports the endurance of feelings and the abandonment of worldliness.

l: Seventh Lecture, Called Liberation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: The Seventh Lecture, Called Liberation, sets rules for mendicants and householders, then explains ascetic restraint through pain, possessions, food, illness, and religious death to diminish sin, dissolve karman, and reach Nirvâna.

l: householders, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Householders may approach mendicants with food, clothing, lodging, or assistance, but must not injure living beings to obtain offerings; those who do are instructed against such obsequiousness.

l: the three vows, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: are_enjoined_by Mahâvîra The three vows are described as having been enjoined by the wise Brahman, Mahâvîra. Noble and tranquil persons who are enlightened and exert themselves in these precepts are called free from sinful acts.

l: desire, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_abandoned_by mendicants [as part of becoming unfettered] Those who are awakened should not wish for pleasure or forbidden things. A person without desires and without harm toward living beings is called unfettered, and the ascetic should not nourish desire or greed for transitory or greater pleasures.

l: Nirvâna, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Nirvâna is the final liberation reached through disciplined detachment and one of three good methods of religious death, after enduring bodily dissolution. Mahâvîra proceeds undisturbed through hardship toward it and ends liberated, free from delusion.

l: religious death, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_a method of entering Nirvâna [adopted by those free from delusion] Religious death is described as a disciplined method in which an ascetic examines a clean place, lies or remains there, bears hunger and pain, and does not harm animals feeding on his body. The unit presents progressively more difficult methods, including restricting bodily motions and remaining immovable.

l: penance, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: suits mendicants [when aspiring to freedom from bonds] Penance suits the mendicant who gives up unnecessary clothing, endures cold, heat, hunger, illness, and other painful feelings, and conforms to what the Revered One declared. It is also connected with reducing food and continuing effort when the body is weak.

l: food, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Mahâvîra ate clean food that had been prepared for somebody else and refused food expressly prepared for him. He accepted rough, stale, moist, dry, cold, or poor food, sometimes ate only at long intervals, and sometimes went weeks or months without drinking.

l: Lâdha, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_a rough country [difficult to travel in] Lâdha was a pathless and rough country where Mahâvîra faced many dangers. Its inhabitants attacked him, and dogs were set upon him and bit him.

l: robe, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Mahâvîra used a robe only during the first winter after entering the order and did not leave it off for a year and a month. He then gave it up, did not use another person's robe, and wandered naked.

l: resting-places, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: Mahâvîra’s resting-places span workshops through burying-grounds and trees, where he meditates, sleeps little, and endures disturbances.

l: dogs, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: attack monks [biting and tearing them] Dogs attacked, bit, and tore many mendicants in Lâdha and were sometimes urged to attack them. Mahâvîra endured such dangers without using a stick or abandoning his restraint.

l: The Pillow of Righteousness, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book I
s: is_a lecture [called the Pillow of Righteousness] The Pillow of Righteousness is the title of the lecture containing these four lessons. It presents the conduct, hardships, restraint, nonviolence, and meditation of the Venerable One as a rule for monks.

The Akaranga Sutra, Book II, translated by Hermann Jacobi, is a comprehensive rulebook for monks, nuns, mendicants, Sramanas, and Nirgranthas. It begins with detailed instructions for begging food: alms must not harm living beings or be impure, specially prepared, improperly offered, or sought through desire, competition, gesture, speech, or favoritism. Mendicants must avoid festivals and unsuitable houses, share food impartially, handle doubtful food, drink, meat, salt, and provisions for sick mendicants by prescribed rules, and respect fellow ascetics who follow differing commands of the Gina. It then governs lodging, walking, speech, clothes, bowls, and possessions, requiring inspection, restraint, permission, non-injury, careful travel, truthful and harmless speech, and limited, suitable property. The Second Part adds rules for postures, study places, easing nature, and avoiding sensory attachment to sounds, colours, forms, care, adornment, and reciprocal bodily services. The Third Part recounts Mahâvîra’s descent, birth, renunciation, twelve years of ascetic practice, attainment of Kevala, Nirvâna, and teaching first to gods and then to men. Mahâvîra teaches Gautama and other Sramanas and Nirgranthas the five great vows: abstaining from killing, lying, taking what is not given, sexual pleasures, and attachments, each with five clauses. The final lecture presents liberation: recognizing temporary residence, abandoning bonds and attachment, enduring suffering and pleasure without harm, and practicing austerity, wisdom, meditation, restraint, and the great vows until one quits the path of births.

l: Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: A sutra whose Second Book opens with a lecture on begging food, setting rules for monks, nuns, and mendicants on alms and conduct.

l: First Lecture, Called Begging of Food, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: A lecture explaining monks’ and nuns’ whole duty in collecting alms: acceptable food, handling impure food, and proper conduct while begging from beginning to end.

is_a mendicant [female] A female mendicant entering a householder's abode to collect alms should not accept food recognised as impure or unacceptable. She should follow the same restrictions as a monk or nun concerning food, movement, and relations with householders and heretics.

The monk is a male mendicant whose life is organized around disciplined begging-tours and strict avoidance of improper food, conduct, and desire. He undertakes and participates in begging-tours, entering a householder’s abode for alms only after food has been prepared and distributed. He accepts food and related offerings from unblamed, uncensured families and at the proper time, including after others at an entertainment have received their share, but refuses offerings made for large communal entertainments when the conditions are improper. He does not travel, enter or leave an abode, wander, or exchange food with a heretic, householder, or a monk who does not avoid forbidden food; he also does not give food to a heretic or householder during a begging-tour. He should not seek food or drink in always liberal, always open houses, nor resolve to attend festive entertainment for food. Attendance at entertainment and entry into a householder’s abode depend on suitable conditions, such as an uncrowded gathering and a route with few living beings, seeds, and obstacles. On tour, he avoids hungry-animal gatherings when a byway exists, avoids improper gestures, speech, posture, and solicitation, and rejects food handled or prepared in prohibited ways. His dietary discipline excludes impure liquor, raw or insufficiently modified food, plants, fruits, grains, dregs, honey, ghee, garlic, specified plants and cooked items, and substances containing or fostering living beings. He must also avoid smelling food, drink, and sweet scents with eagerness, desire, greed, or covetousness. Overall, the records present a mendicant governed by careful alms-taking, nonassociation with improper companions, and extensive rules protecting purity and restraint.

A nun is a female mendicant and ascetic whose life is governed by disciplined begging, travel, food, conduct, contemplation, speech, and restraint from sensory attachment. She undertakes and uses begging-tours, enters a householder’s abode for alms only under proper conditions, and accepts food that is pure, acceptable, and respectfully given. She avoids food affected by living beings or impurities, refuses âdhâkarmika food, does not select food by smell, consumes what she receives, and consults fellow-ascetics before rejecting excess. She must avoid seeking food or drink in houses of nearer or remoter relations and observe restrictions concerning houses, householders, and food prepared for others. She does not travel with a householder and moves carefully between villages or across water, especially during appropriate seasons and conditions, so as not to harm living beings or accept unsuitable help. When threatened or disturbed, she collects herself for contemplation and stays apart where people do not pass or see her. Her speech must be deliberate, precise, moderate, restrained, and free from wrath, pride, deception, gain, roughness, divisiveness, or harm; non-truth-or-untruth speech is permitted only when not sinful or blamable. Finally, she must not go to walls or ditches to hear sounds, seek entertainments improperly, or delight in sounds of either world.

A householder is a person with an abode whose household may be approached by a monk or nun while begging. The householder gives or prepares food for mendicants and others, sometimes out of respect for a Nirgrantha or for a fellow-ascetic, but such offerings may be unacceptable when bought, stolen, forcibly taken, prepared through injury to living beings, altered for the mendicant, given with certain hands, or prepared over fire. For a mendicant’s sake, the householder may alter small or large doors, reposition beds, cut grass, spread a couch, and use stools, benches, ladders, or a handmill to fetch food. These acts may involve falling, breaking earthen vessels, injuring earth-, fire-, or wind-bodies, or processing liquor by pressing, straining, or filtering. The records therefore present the householder as a provider whose assistance can also create impurity, injury, sin, and reasons for a well-controlled Nirgrantha to avoid a festival with a feast.
A monk or nun should not enter or leave a householder's abode, practise outside, wander from village to village, or exchange food together with a heretic.

A fellow-ascetic is an agreeable, unshunned companion governed by rules of conduct. Nearby fellow-ascetics who follow the same rules may receive food or drink an inadvertently accepting mendicant cannot consume. A zealous brother following the same rules may be invited to collected food; those following other rules may be offered begged furnishings, but not something possessed for somebody else.

Nirgrantha is a well-controlled mendicant, described through rules governing conduct on a begging-tour and the handling of alms. The account begins with respect received from a householder when food is given, but stresses restraint: Nirgrantha should avoid festive or vulgar entertainments, since liquor, sickness, loss of mindfulness, and improper sexual pursuit may follow. On tour, the mendicant avoids obstacles, dangerous beings, unsafe ground, and other beggars or mendicants when an alternative route exists; obtains permission before passing, clearing, entering, or leaving a secured householder’s entrance; and cleans bodily contamination only with suitable begged materials in a secluded, examined place. Food must be shared impartially. Acceptance of food and water requires scrutiny of how it was obtained, prepared, fetched, altered, or strained. Impure, unacceptable, specially procured, or inefficiently edible items, including âdhâkarmika food, sugar-cane, pea-pods, and seed-pods, must be refused. The mendicant also avoids nearer and remoter relations’ houses and accepts suitable alms given out of respect for the cloth. Finally, alms gathered for many require consultation with spiritual authorities, teacher, sub-teacher, religious guide, Sthavira, head of a Gana, Ganadhara, or founder of a Gana, and distribution as directed, without concealing or reserving better food. Inadvertent acceptance of prohibited food or salt calls for prescribed eating, disposal, permission, or sharing procedures.

Sramanas are mendicants governed by vows of renunciation and detailed rules of conduct. They own no house, property, sons, or cattle; eat what others give; and renounce accepting anything not given. They may receive food prepared for many persons and lodging alongside guests, paupers, beggars, and Brâhmanas, but must not take an unfair share, obstruct another Sramana, or appropriate a traveller's hall without permission. Their begging is regulated: they should obtain acceptable alms from other families, avoid doubtful food, and reject food from certain households. They must not seek festivals, entertainments, or pleasing sights such as colours and forms. They travel, enter households, and undertake religious practice with a complete outfit except in unsuitable weather or insect conditions. To avoid occasions of sin, a mendicant may choose one of four rules for religious postures and stand accordingly. Thus the records move from conduct in food, travel, and lodging to strict renunciation, possession, religious posture, and avoidance of sensory pleasure.
Brâhmanas are recipients of food prepared by a householder for many persons, but not when only part may be used; monks and nuns must respect their presence and take no more than an impartial share.

A beggar may already have entered a householder's abode or may join in receiving and sharing food. The monk or nun should join the other beggars when food is given for all, and should divide or eat it equally without preference.

l: abode of a householder, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The abode of a householder is a place where food may be offered to monks or nuns collecting alms. They must inspect and reject impure food, enter with a complete outfit, and avoid entering or leaving with it during strong rain, mist, dust, or many flying insects.
A secluded place is one where no people pass or see the monk or nun and where eggs or living beings are absent. It is the prescribed place for easing nature with a chamber-pot.

Monks and nuns enter or leave out-of-door places for religious practices or study with the complete outfit. They should not enter or leave them under the listed conditions of strong rain, widespread mist, high wind with dust, or many flying insects.

A village is assessed as a place for monks or nuns to stay or travel through. Its key value is providing religious-practice or study space, adequate necessities, and acceptable alms. During the rainy season, they should remain in a suitably equipped village; during the cold season, they should not remain where facilities and means of existence are lacking. They must not go there for entertainment.

A householder's abode is a lodging used by a householder, containing family, cattle, food, drink, and features such as doors, bathroom, privy, loopholes, fissures, and secured entrances. Monks or nuns must remain unseen while cows are milked and food is prepared or distributed, then enter or leave circumspectly for alms. They need permission, examination, and sweeping to pass a thorn-secured entrance. They should not use the lodging for postures, study, or rest while household people, animals, provisions, fire, or water are present, lest improper dependence or involvement arise.

Food is assessed for purity and acceptability in offerings to monks or nuns. It is impure and unacceptable if affected or mixed with living beings, mildew, seeds or sprouts, water, dust, or other listed impurities; it is also unacceptable when fetched from above or placed on specified supports or bodies, including vegetable or animal matter. Herbs, grains, and flour may be accepted after their source of life is absent or they have been worked more than once. Food prepared by a giver for large gatherings, festivals, or communal entertainments is generally impure, while food prepared by another person may be acceptable and pure under the stated conditions. Food from Kshatriyas, kings, messengers, or relations of kings is impure and unacceptable. A monk or nun should refuse food if its status causes doubt. Food given for Sramanas or beggars must be silently accepted and impartially divided or eaten equally, without choosing desirable portions. Food may be discarded, distributed, eaten, deferred, or already removed; food cooled by a layman blowing or fanning for the mendicant should not be accepted.

Drink has well-flavoured and astringent parts. A monk or nun should consume all received drink without rejection, offer any excess to nearby agreeable fellow-ascetics, and follow seven rules, with an exception for lightly cleaned water used to water flour or sesamum.

Alms concern food, drink, dainties, and spices obtained on a begging-tour. They may be accepted only when pure and acceptable. Food procured through theft, force, sinful conduct, or preparations for ascetics must be rejected. Monks and nuns should seek other families when entertainment food would cause sin. Alms from Kshatriyas, kings, messengers, or kings’ relations are impure and unacceptable.

Living beings are sentient entities that can affect food, liquor, and lodging places. They experience all kinds of sensation, temporarily reside in one of four states of being, and include six classes such as earth-body and animals. They may be harmed during food fetching, vessel breaking, or tending fire; such actions, and sinful conduct toward them, make food unacceptable. The account ends by requiring that they not be killed, injured, displaced, or treated with attachment or aversion.

Water, hot or cold, may contain living beings and is governed by rules of acceptance and crossing. Water from bare ground, associated with cobwebs, recently used for watering flour, sesamum, rice, or washing, or fetched in a wet, moist, or dirty vessel mixed with cold water is unacceptable. Changed, strained water used long ago may be accepted. A monk or nun crosses circumspectly and dries naturally after swimming or wading.
Eggs make ground unfit for easing nature. Monks and nuns should ease nature only where the ground is free from eggs or living beings.

The Eleventh Lesson sets seven rules for mendicants accepting food. Food for a sick mendicant must not be concealed or misrepresented for eating. Acceptance depends on wet or dry hands and vessels, cleaning, moisture, food from the ground, and portions unwanted by others; food ground or winnowed on living material is impure and unacceptable.

A begging-tour is the alms-collecting activity undertaken by a monk or nun, chiefly a regulated setting for seeking and receiving food, water, drink, raw substances, and other offerings. It begins with restrictions on companionship: the mendicant must not travel with certain persons or give them food. Food acceptability is central: offerings connected with entertainments, wedding breakfasts, funeral or family dinners, specified households, guests, sick persons, fire preparation, impurity, or doubt must be avoided. The tour may pass entertainments or householders only under prescribed conditions, with indifference to festival entertainment. Its route must avoid numerous living beings, seeds, sprouts, dew, water, mildew, dust, cobwebs, and obstructing people. Along the way, the monk or nun encounters houses, other alms recipients, obstacles, dangerous beings, animals, and householders; a byway is required when available, and the mendicant waits apart before entering a house already entered by another recipient. The tour concludes in regulated acceptance of portions, without preference, under rules governing sources, preparation, gestures, salt, and offerings.
When collecting alms, a monk or nun should examine offered food and accept only what is pure and acceptable. They should not enter or leave a householder's abode with prohibited companions.

The whole duty is the complete prescribed discipline for a monk or nun: rules on food, alms, conduct, and continual exertion. Stated in the Eighth Lesson, it requires understanding all meanings, bliss, rejecting specified impure or raw substances, and indifference to pleasant scents.

A householder gives and prepares lodging for mendicants; preparing, altering, cleaning, furnishing, or surrendering it may make it unsuitable or affected by sins and create occasions for attachment, approval, dislike, or sexual temptation.

A monk is an ascetic and mendicant whose life is governed by shared rules of conduct, careful begging, nonattachment, and circumspect wandering. He lives in villages or wanders from village to village, sometimes being directed with fellow mendicants to outlying villages to beg alms. Though he may have kinsmen or relations, he does not enter their houses for food or drink, does not seek provisions before begging, and accepts alms only at the proper time and when respectfully given. He possesses an alms-bowl, eats what he receives without selecting by smell, rejects food prepared specifically for him, and consults fellow ascetics before refusing excess food. Begging food and drink follows seven rules, while different compliant rules are to be respected as efforts under the commandment of the Gina. His lodging, couch, posture, rest, and study require inspection, cleaning, and fitness: places must contain few eggs or living beings, and couches must be safe, movable, and well tied. He avoids householders' quarters, improper lodgings, and prolonged stays in halting-places, while asking about ownership before seeking lodging. During travel and the rainy season, he proceeds carefully through villages, roads, and water, avoiding injury to living beings, unsuitable aid, and involvement in householders' activities. When threatened or disturbed, he practices contemplation. Finally, he avoids going to walls or ditches to hear sounds and does not seek, like, or become enraptured with sounds of either world.

A festive entertainment is an assembly setting that entertains many people, sometimes feeding Sramanas, Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars on communal or religious occasions. It may chiefly serve meat, fish, or roasted slices and involve liquors. For monks and nuns, it is not a reason or destination for travel, especially beyond half a yogana; after learning its location, they should go the opposite way. They should not plan to attend when linked with a feast or entertainment, particularly with such food, though suitable route and assembly conditions may permit attendance.

is small [described as too populous and not large] A village may be described as small, too populous, or not large. When a village is considered unsuitable for begging, mendicants may be told to go to outlying villages.

The Kevalin is an omniscient authority and teacher who gives reasons for religious restrictions. He explains why to reject food prepared over fire, inspect robes for hidden things or living matter, and judge lodging fitness. Across the lessons, he warns that food at entertainments may involve sinful preparation or acquisition; entertainments with feasts risk illness, sensual temptation, and sin; and food from elevated places, broken earthenware, or disturbed fire can harm living beings and incur sin.

A couch may be accepted by a monk or nun only if free of eggs and living beings, light, movable, and well tied. Heavy, immovable, badly tied couches are unacceptable; one with few living beings may be returned after inspection, sweeping, and drying.

Sin is said to multiply continuously through entertainments, food, mixed company, drunken sensual pursuits, unsuitable food, and harmful speech; it unfolds by naming causes and then urging monks and nuns to avoid destructive speech through restrained, careful words.
A lesson on lodging restrictions concerning clothing: monks and nuns beg for acceptable clothes, wear them unchanged, regulate their handling, and learn how to act when encountering thieves.
is_a lesson The Third Lesson sets out rules concerning festive entertainments, feasts, alms, food, travel, and the conduct of monks and nuns.

Nuns are mendicants governed by a third lesson on conduct. They must not seek festivals, feasts, or village entertainment; instead they obtain acceptable alms from other families, avoid doubtful or prohibited food, and reject food from houses connected to Kshatriyas, kings, messengers, or kings’ relations. They wear a complete outfit when entering homes, traveling, or religious practice and study, except in harsh outdoor conditions.
A feast associated with a festive entertainment may create circumstances leading to illness or sin. Monks and nuns should not resolve to attend a festival that is preceded or followed by a feast.
A woman is described through proper forms of address: she should not receive abusive or degrading speech, especially when silent, but respectful terms including sister and lay-sister.

l: much-frequented and vulgar entertainment, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: causes injury [through crowding and unacceptable exchanges] A much-frequented and vulgar entertainment may cause bodily collisions, blows, dust, cold water, unacceptable food, or receipt of something meant for others. A well-controlled Nirgrantha should not resolve to go to such an entertainment to partake of it.

A monk or nun should wear the complete outfit when entering a householder’s abode, entering or leaving out-of-door places for religious practices or study, and wandering from village to village. They should not perform these actions with the complete outfit when strong rain, widespread mist, high wind with much dust, or many flying insects are present.

Clothes are classified by whether a mendicant may accept them. Acceptable clothes, begged for in the prescribed way, may be wool, silk, hemp, palm-leaves, cotton, Arkatûla, or similar materials and must be fit, strong, lasting, wearable, pleasant, and free from impurities. Appropriated, expensive, ornate, or impure clothes must not be accepted; clothes are not washed or dyed because they are not new.

l: meat or fish, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Meat or fish containing many bones is impure and unacceptable when most must be rejected; if accepted inadvertently, eat the edible part suitably and leave bones secluded on ashes.

A householder is a resident whose home and conduct shape a mendicant’s alms and care. Their abode should not be entered during milking or before cooked food is distributed, and mendicants must not visit relatives in expectation of food. A householder may procure, prepare, permit, or knowingly give certain food, subject to rules on âdhâkarmika food and salt. They may also offer bodily care, ornaments, charms, and plant-cutting treatments to mendicants.

is_given_for cloth [out of respect] Alms may be accepted at the proper time from families when they are acceptable and given out of respect for the mendicant’s cloth. A mendicant should not arrange beforehand to obtain food or other provisions from related families before begging.

is_a impure and unacceptable substance [when containing particles of shell, skin, or seeds and processed for the mendicant] Liquor containing particles of shell, skin, or seeds, even when pressed, strained, or filtered for the mendicant, is impure and unacceptable. Old liquor or liquor in which living beings are engendered, grow, thrive, remain, or are killed or destroyed should not be accepted.

An alms-bowl may be made of bottle-gourd, wood, or clay, and may be used, left off, or unwanted by others. Expensive materials or bands, food or drink, and cold water offered by the householder make it impure and unacceptable. It is inspected, emptied of living beings or seeds, wiped dry, and protected from moisture and heavy rain.

l: division of food, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Division of food is an impartial, equal distribution: a monk or nun avoids selecting disproportionately large, preferred vegetables or conspicuous, savoury, delicious, nice, or big things, without eagerness, desire, greed, or covetousness.

includes eager or greedy taking [in dividing or eating food] It is sinful for a monk or nun to hurry toward food being taken or eaten, to take an excessive or desirable share, or to eat food given for all as though it were only for the monk or nun. It is also sinful to disregard the prescribed avoidance, permission, cleaning, and sharing practices.

is_a lesson The Sixth Lesson sets out rules for monks and nuns on a begging-tour, including how they should behave around animals, houses, householders, and food. It teaches that certain food and salt are impure and unacceptable, especially when prepared or altered for the mendicant’s sake.

Food is governed by rules of purity, acceptance, preparation, receipt, consumption, disclosure, and distribution. It is impure and unacceptable when given from a hand, pot, spoon, or plate treated with cold or hot water, but pure and acceptable when a similarly soiled hand gives it to a similarly soiled or unsoiled recipient. Food prepared over fire, or certain grains or salts ground or pounded for a mendicant, should not be accepted. It should also not be accepted when prepared for a mendicant or another without permission, or placed before a relation’s house. Monk and nun must consume received sweet-smelling or bad-smelling food, consult before rejecting excess, disclose food, avoid concealment, and distribute food collected for many after consultation.
Fossil salt is impure and unacceptable when ground or pounded for a mendicant on living material; brought from a householder, it must be knowingly given before consumption or division.
Sea salt is impure and unacceptable when ground or pounded for a mendicant on living material; brought from a householder, it must be knowingly given before consumption or division.

has_part fire-bodies Fire is described as consisting of fire-bodies that a layman may kill by wetting, moistening, wiping, rubbing, throwing up, or turning down food prepared over it for the mendicant. For this reason, food prepared over fire is impure and unacceptable.

Animals include deer, cattle, birds, snakes, and aquatic animals. They originate and become numerous in the rainy season, occurring in many places. Monks and nuns should avoid injuring or disturbing them and avoid things containing living beings.

Ground is unsuitable for easing nature when it is infected by eggs or living beings, prepared for a monk or nun, occupied by force, covered or treated, wet, dusty, or otherwise containing life. Suitable ground must be inspected and cleaned and must be away from specified public, cultivated, sacred, or dangerous places.
is_a lesson The Eighth Lesson teaches rules governing what a monk or nun on a begging-tour may accept, smell, or reject. It concludes with the declaration that this is the whole duty.

A mango has peel, rind, and sap. For monks or nuns, it may be taken only when free from eggs and living beings and nibbled by animals or injured; mangoes covered with eggs or living beings, or uninjured and untouched, are impure and prohibited.

is_a impure and unacceptable substance [when not yet modified by instruments] Raw things that have not been modified by instruments, including roots, spices, fruits, shoots, berries, plants, vegetables, seeds, sprouts, and other substances, should not be accepted. Raw things are unacceptable when they are unmodified, poorly ground, contain small seeds, or are otherwise described as impure.
is_a lesson The Ninth Lesson sets out rules for mendicants, monks, and nuns concerning the acceptance and consumption of food and drink.
Ascetics are praised as illustrious, pious, virtuous, eloquent, restrained, controlled, and chaste, having ceased sensual intercourse; nearby fellow-ascetics may offer excessive food or drink.
Faithful householders, residing in all directions and possessing vessels, may offer ready food to ascetics; such âdhâkarmika food should not be accepted.

is_a mendicant [sick] A sick mendicant may be given agreeable food received by another mendicant. Food that is unsuitable for the sick mendicant should be identified by its pungent, bitter, astringent, sour, or sweet parts rather than being falsely presented as wholly unfit.

Pilgrimage is wandering from village to village, sometimes through forest despite thieves. A monk or nun should choose safer routes when available and avoid answering travellers’ questions about anything encountered along the way.
is_a lesson The Tenth Lesson sets out duties concerning the collection, distribution, acceptance, consumption, and sharing of alms by mendicants and nuns.

l: impurity and unacceptability, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Impurity and unacceptability apply to partly edible sugar-cane and pods, meat or fish with many bones, and fossil salt or sea salt offered in the specified circumstances. Such items should generally not be accepted, though the text prescribes special procedures for items accepted inadvertently.

l: seven rules for begging food, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The seven rules govern accepting begged food, considering the mendicant’s hand and vessel, required cleaning, the giver’s wet hands, food from the ground, usable portions, and others’ wishes.

l: seven rules for begging drink, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Seven rules for begging drink resemble seven rules for begging food, except the fourth addresses accepting water used for watering flour or sesamum requiring little cleaning or removal of impure articles.
Gina, an infinite knowing one who illumines three worlds, is the source of commandments guiding mendicants to exert themselves and respect one another, and proclaimed great vows throughout the earth.

A lodging-place for religious posture must be inspected and cleaned, contain only few eggs or living beings, and avoid harmful preparation for the mendicant. It becomes unsuitable when prepared for the mendicant or when above ground, underground, householders’ space, inaccessible, dangerous, frequently visited, or sinfully prepared.

Religious postures are practices for monks or nuns, permitted only in suitably pure and safe lodging-places or couches, not householders’ lodgings or unsuitable places. They unfold through four rules governing leaning, changing position, slight movement, or complete motionlessness.

l: begging for a couch, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: is_governed_by four rules for begging for a couch [for avoidance of occasions to sin] When begging for a couch, a monk or nun should specify or inspect the requested couch and address the householder respectfully. If the couch is not obtained under the applicable rule, the mendicant should remain in a squatting or sitting posture for the night.

l: four rules for begging for a couch, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: govern begging for a couch [four rules] The four rules permit a monk or nun to beg for a specified couch, to beg after inspecting it, to request it from the person whose house is occupied, or to request a couch as it is spread on the ground or a wooden plank. These rules govern when the couch may be used and require the mendicant to remain squatting or sitting if it is not obtained.

Lodging fitness concerns whether a lodging-place suits mendicant use. It requires inspection of the lodging and floor, avoiding harmful beings, unsuitable activity, improper preparation, danger, obstruction, and excessive associations; the mendicant remains content despite discomforts.

A lesson on lodging restrictions concerns clothes begging and use, prescribing acceptable clothes for monks and nuns, inspection and impurity standards, four begging rules, and rules for airing or drying clothes.

l: Third Lecture, Called Walking, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: A lecture teaching monks and nuns conduct during rain, pilgrimage, and wandering, emphasizing avoidance of harm, danger, unnecessary speech, and disturbing living beings.

A road may contain living beings, seeds, grass, water, mud, walls, ditches, ramparts, or gates and pass through forest. During rainy season, avoid taking it straight when an unobstructed byway exists; avoid dangerous roads when another route is available.
A boat plies a river up, down, or across and may contain water when leaking or sinking. Monks or nuns may enter it with permission and preparation, but must not operate, repair, bail, or stop leaks.
Rainy season is a four-month season when living beings and seeds arise, roads become difficult, and monks and nuns remain in one place until travel is permitted.

l: wandering from village to village, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: requires circumspection It should be done circumspectly, with the monk or nun looking forward for four cubits, choosing byways when appropriate, and avoiding living beings and obstacles. They should not converse unnecessarily with householders, reveal information to travellers, or seek refuge from animals, thieves, or other dangers.

is_a religious practice It is used when a monk or a nun faces danger, disturbance, or possible violence. With the mind not directed outwardly, the mendicant should remain undisturbed and collect themselves for contemplation.

A monk is a mendicant and fellow-ascetic governed by detailed disciplines of speech, possessions, movement, study, religious practice, and bodily conduct. Most importantly, the monk must avoid harmful conduct and places containing eggs or living beings. Speech must be true and accurate when not sinful or blamable, precise, moderate, restrained, and free of wrath, pride, deceit, greed, roughness, division, or harm. The monk may obtain limited clothing and, if youthful, strong, healthy, and well-set, wear one robe; clothes must be requested directly, worn as received, and protected. The monk may carry one inspected bowl, travel no farther than half a Yogana for it, clean it only when dry, carry it for alms, and protect it in heavy rain. For religious postures and study, the monk enters a village or suitable town and accepts only places free from eggs or living beings. As a fellow-ascetic, the monk uses a broom, avoids easing nature on living, prepared, harmful, public, sacred, cultivated, or inhabited places, and instead uses a chamber-pot in a secluded, life-free place, leaving excrement on ashes in a secluded spot.
Speech has four kinds, truth, untruth, mixed truth and untruth, or neither, and passes from non-existence before utterance to real speech while uttered and non-existence afterward.

l: modes of speech, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The modes of speech include truth, untruth, truth mixed with untruth, and speech that is neither truth nor untruth. They are to be used with careful judgment, precision, moderation, and restraint.

is_a kind of speech [first] Truth is one of the four kinds of speech taught and declared by all past, present, and future Arhats. A monk or nun should use true and accurate speech when it is not sinful or harmful.

is_a kind of speech [second] Untruth is one of the four kinds of speech taught and declared by all past, present, and future Arhats. A monk or nun should not use untruth when it is sinful, blamable, harsh, divisive, or harmful.

l: truth mixed with untruth, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: is_a kind of speech [third] Truth mixed with untruth is one of the four kinds of speech taught and declared by all past, present, and future Arhats. It should not be used when it is sinful, blamable, harsh, divisive, or harmful.

l: speech that is neither truth nor untruth, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: is_a kind of speech [fourth] Speech that is neither truth nor untruth is identified as the fourth kind of speech, including injunctions. A monk or nun should use it when it is not sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, or otherwise harmful.

teach four kinds of speech [past, present, and future Arhats] All past, present, and future Arhats have taught and declared, teach and declare, and will teach and declare the four kinds of speech. They have also explained things possessing colour, smell, taste, touch, and various qualities.
A man is described as strong and handsome and should be addressed respectfully as a long-lived one or layman, rather than with abusive, degrading, or insulting speech when he does not answer.

has_quality good or bad [according to its nature] Sounds include those of drums, stringed instruments, kettledrums, wind instruments, singing, music, performances, quarrels, festivals, and other activities. Monks and nuns should not go for the sake of hearing them or become enraptured with them.

l: Fifth Lecture, Called Begging of Clothes, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: A lecture teaching rules on monks, nuns, clothing, begging, wearing, and protecting clothes, unfolding through First and Second Lessons.

A nun is a mendicant and fellow-ascetic governed by detailed rules for clothing, bowls, religious practice, study, and bodily needs. She should possess four raiments of prescribed widths and may beg for specified materials, but should not travel farther than half a yogana for clothes or a bowl. Clothes are worn as received and protected from rain; when seeking alms she must be properly clothed and avoid entering or leaving houses during strong, widespread rain. She may carry one bowl if youthful and may beg for a permitted bottle-gourd, wooden, or clay bowl, but not one bought specifically for her. Before using or carrying it into or out of a householder's abode, she inspects it, removes living beings, and wipes off dust; wet bowls are not rubbed until dry. For religious postures she enters a scot-free town, and for study she accepts only places free of eggs or living beings. If lacking her own broom, she may use or beg a fellow-ascetic's. In easing nature, she avoids ground containing life, appropriated or specially prepared places, uses a chamber-pot, chooses a secluded place free of eggs or living beings, and leaves excrement on ashes in a secluded spot.

A householder is a giver and authority over possessions and dwelling-places in rules concerning mendicants. The householder may promise or give clothes, but clothes altered through prohibited washing, dyeing, perfuming, cleaning, rubbing, or other acts must be refused. The householder may give a permitted bowl, arrange its preparation, or ask a mendicant to return later, but must not provide one filled with cooked or prepared food or drink; cold water and food-filled bowls are refused. The householder or steward may grant possession of a dwelling-place and lend small implements that must be returned indirectly. Finally, if the householder kills beings or commits sins in preparing or using a place, informed monks or nuns must not ease nature there or in a similar place.

l: clothes begging rules, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Four rules for begging clothes cover specified cloth qualities, well-inspected clothes, under or upper garments, and unwanted left-off robes. The second lesson addresses robe inspection and prohibits borrowing a robe; acceptable pure clothes received under these rules may be accepted.

l: airing or drying clothes, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: A monastic rule for airing or drying clothes: a monk or nun must use a secluded, repeatedly inspected and cleaned heap of ashes or bones, and must avoid bare ground, wet earth, living clay, houses, and unstable or elevated places.

l: Begging for a Bowl, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: is_a lecture Begging for a Bowl sets out rules for monks and nuns who seek, accept, inspect, carry, and use alms-bowls. It prescribes four permitted ways of begging for a bowl and explains which bowls and offerings are impure and unacceptable.

l: Seventh Lecture, Called Regulation of Possession, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: A lecture outlines two lessons regulating mendicants’ acquisition and use of dwellings, food, implements, and other property.

l: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra is a Gñâtri Kshatriya of Kâsyapa gotra, born in Kundapura after descending from heaven and being transferred from Devânandâ’s womb to Trisalâ’s. Son of Siddhartha and Trisalâ, he was named Vardhamâna, lived thirty years as a householder, with Yasodâ, Anoggâ, and Seshavatî named among his family. He renounced the world, practiced asceticism for twelve years, gained Manahparyâya knowledge, and attained Kevala outside Grimbhikagrâma. As an Arhat and Kevalin, omniscient and endowed with highest knowledge and intuition, he first taught gods and then men, including the five great vows, six classes of lives, and fivefold dominion.

is_a domicile [a place where mendicants may stay with permission] A traveller's hall is a place where a mendicant may beg for a domicile after reflecting on its fitness and obtaining permission from its landlord or steward. The mendicant may occupy only the time and space conceded and should avoid disturbing or offending its inmates.
Dominion is classified fivefold: the lord of the gods’, king’s, houseowner’s, householder’s, and religious man’s dominions, as declared by the Sthaviras and explained by Mahâvîra.

l: seven rules of possession, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Seven rules of possession govern how monks and nuns request, take possession of, and use dwelling-places. They begin with asking for a domicile after considering its fitness, distinguish possession and use for oneself or other mendicants, address a place ceded to others, limit asking for one’s own sake, and end with permitted use of obtained Ikkada reed and clay- or wood-paved dwellings.

is_a dominion [one of the subjects classified as fivefold] Possession must be obtained with permission from the person who controls the place or object, and it is limited to the time, space, and number of fellow-ascetics conceded. Mendicants must not take what has not been given, must avoid unsuitable or harmful locations, and must not use possessions obtained for somebody else.
is_called Seven Lectures The Second Part ends with this unit.

l: The Seven Lectures, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The Second Part is called the Seven Lectures.
is_a lecture The Eighth Lecture sets out rules for monks and nuns who wish to perform religious postures. It describes four possible rules for standing.

l: four rules for the performance of religious postures, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The four rules progressively move from leaning and slight movement while changing position to standing without leaning, changing position, or movement, demanding increasing stillness.
The first rule directs a mendicant to choose something inanimate for support, lean against it, change body position, and move a little while standing.
The second rule directs a mendicant to lean on something inanimate, change body position, and remain standing without moving about a little.
The third rule directs the mendicant to lean on something inanimate while standing without changing body position or moving about.

The fourth rule has a mendicant choose something inanimate without leaning against it, remain perfectly motionless without changing bodily position or moving even a little, and abandon care of the body, hair, beard, other body parts, and nails.
is_a lecture The Ninth Lecture sets out rules for monks and nuns choosing a place for study and for parties of mendicants traveling there.

l: place for study, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: A place for study is impure and unacceptable when infected by eggs or living beings; free from them, it is pure and acceptable, subject to stated couch rules through “water-plants.”

l: parties of two, three, four, or five (mendicants), Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: do_not_harm body (of the mendicants) [by embracing, hugging, biting with their teeth, or scratching with their nails] Parties of two, three, four, or five mendicants who resolve to go to the place for study should not embrace or hug, bite each other with their teeth, or scratch each other with their nails.
is_a lecture The Tenth Lecture sets out rules for monks and nuns concerning easing nature. It specifies unsuitable grounds and places and prescribes the use of a chamber-pot in a secluded place.
Nature easing should not be done on unsuitable, inhabited, cultivated, sacred, public, or harmful places. It should be done with a chamber-pot in a secluded place free from eggs and living beings.

A monk or nun should take their own chamber-pot or that of somebody else. They should carry it to a secluded place, ease nature there, and then leave the excrements on a heap of ashes or a similar spot.

Great festivals may involve well-dressed and ornamented women and men singing, making music, dancing, laughing, playing, sporting, and distributing food, drink, dainties, and spices. Monks and nuns should not go to such festivals for the sake of hearing sounds.
A lecture teaching monks and nuns not to seek pleasing colours or forms, then repeating prior instructions about sounds while omitting music passages.

should_not_resolve_to_go where they will see various colours (or forms) [for the sake of pleasing the eye] A nun should not resolve to go where she will see various colours or forms merely to please the eye. These colours or forms may appear in wreaths, dressed images, dolls, clothes, woodwork, plastering, paintings, jewelry, ivory-work, strings, or leaf-cutting.

l: various colours (or forms), Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Various colours or forms appear in decorative and crafted objects; monks and nuns should not deliberately seek them merely to please the eye.

A lecture instructs a mendicant not to welcome or forbid karmic actions by others, surveys care and cures, explains sensation as arising from former actions, and is to be repeated for reciprocal actions.

Mendicant is a person governed by prohibitions on approving or forbidding others’ bodily care, reciprocal acts, and cures directed at him. The account first covers washing, grooming, decorating, postures, places, charms, and living plant materials; it then narrows to reciprocal actions producing karman, including mutual wiping or rubbing of feet.
Karman is produced by others’ actions relating to a mendicant and by reciprocal action; the mendicant should neither approve nor prohibit them.
results_from former actions Sensation is the result of former actions. All sorts of living beings experience sensation.

repeats Thirteenth Lecture [the whole lecture] The Fourteenth Lecture teaches that one should neither be pleased with nor prohibit reciprocal actions relating to oneself and producing karman. It repeats the whole Thirteenth Lecture in this way.
Reciprocal action relating to oneself produces karman and should neither be welcomed nor prohibited, exemplified by wiping or rubbing feet.

l: Mahâvîra's descent from heaven, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Mahâvîra's descent from Pushpottara Vimâna occurs after twenty Sâgaropamas, ending in Kundapura in Gambûdvîpa while the moon is in Uttaraphalgunî.

l: Mahâvîra's conception in Devânandâ's womb, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Mahâvîra descended from heaven and became an embryo in Devânandâ’s womb, knowing before and after the descent but not its infinitesimally small moment.

belongs_to_gotra Gâlandharâyana gotra Devânandâ belonged to the Gâlandharâyana gotra and was the wife of the Brâhmana Rishabhadatta. Mahâvîra was first conceived in her womb, and later the fetus of Trisalâ was lodged in her womb.

l: Mahâvîra's transfer from Devânandâ's womb to Trisalâ's womb, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: On the eighty-third day, Indra compassionately transfers Mahâvîra’s embryo from Devânandâ’s womb to Trisalâ’s, retaining clean matter and exchanging Trisalâ’s fetus into Devânandâ’s womb.
Trisalâ, of the Vâsishtha gotra and wife of Siddhartha, received Mahâvîra’s embryo and, after nine months and seven and a half days, gave birth to him under Uttaraphalgunî.
Mahâvîra's birth to healthy Kshatriyânî Trisalâ occurs in Kundapura during dark Kaitra, under Uttaraphalgunî, marked by divine lustre, gods, showers, and auspicious ceremonies.

l: gods and goddesses, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Gods and goddesses from four classes attend Mahâvîra’s birth with lustre, offerings, and anointment; later they support his renunciation, accompany his palankin with music, and descend and ascend at his Kevala.

l: anointment as a Tîrthakara, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The gods and goddesses performed the customary ceremonies of auspiciousness and honour and anointed Mahâvîra as a Tîrthakara on the night of his birth.

l: Mahâvîra's renunciation of household life, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Mahâvîra’s renunciation of household life follows thirty years among householders and a year of giving away wealth. In Gñâtri Shanda under Uttaraphalgunî, he leaves Kundapura, removes ornaments, plucks out five handfuls of hair, honors liberated spirits, and adopts holy conduct.

Sakra, leader and king of the gods, magically creates a divine pavilion and throne, bathes and adorns Mahâvîra, produces Kandraprabhâ, catches his hair, and ends clamour and music at his holy conduct.

l: Mahâvîra's palankin Kandraprabhâ, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Kandraprabhâ, produced by Sakra, is a richly decorated palankin carried by a thousand men, transporting Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra from Kundapura to Gñâtri Shanda.

l: Mahâvîra's adoption of holy conduct, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: follows Mahâvîra's renunciation of household life [after plucking out his hair] After plucking out his hair and paying obeisance to liberated spirits, Mahâvîra vowed to do no sinful act and adopted holy conduct. He resolved to neglect his body for twelve years and to endure calamities with equanimity.

knows thoughts of all sentient beings [with five non-defective organs and developed intellect] After adopting holy conduct, Mahâvîra reached Manahparyâya knowledge. Through it he knew the thoughts of sentient beings with five unimpaired organs and developed intellects living in the two and a half continents and the two oceans.

l: Nirvâna and liberation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Nirvâna and liberation is Mahâvîra’s path through restraint and virtues, culminating in a complete, unobstructed, infinite, supreme state.

l: Mahâvîra's attainment of Kevala, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: is highest knowledge and intuition [complete, full, unobstructed, unimpeded, infinite and supreme] During the thirteenth year, outside Grimbhikagrâma near the river Rigupâlikâ, Mahâvîra attained Kevala in deep meditation. He became an Arhat and Gina, omniscient and comprehending all objects and all conditions of the world.

l: highest knowledge and intuition, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The highest knowledge and intuition called Kevala is described as infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and perfect. Mahâvîra obtained it while the moon was in conjunction with Uttaraphalgunî.
After attaining the highest knowledge and intuition, Mahâvîra reflected on himself and the world. He first taught the law to the gods and afterward to men.

contains Kundapura [place of Mahâvîra's conception, transfer, birth and renunciation] Gambûdvîpa was the continent in which Mahâvîra descended, was conceived, and later renounced household life. Kundapura was located there in Bharatavarsha.

Kundapura contained the southern brahmanical part where Mahâvîra was first conceived and the northern Kshatriya part where he was transferred to Trisalâ’s womb. Mahâvîra was born there and later departed from its northern Kshatriya part in the palankin Kandraprabhâ.

is_conjoined_with moon [during Mahâvîra's major life events] Uttaraphalgunî was the asterism accompanying Mahâvîra’s descent from heaven, conception, transfer between wombs, birth, renunciation, and attainment of Kevala. The text identifies these as five important moments of his life, while final liberation occurred in Svâti.

Nirgranthas are Houseless when well provided with the five great vows and their twenty-five clauses. Instructed by the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra, they correctly practise the vows, beginning with abstinence from killing living beings. Their discipline unfolds through careful walking, examination of mind and speech, and deliberation in speaking, begging, handling utensils, and consuming inspected food and drink with permission. They renounce anger, greed, fear, mirth, sexual pleasures, and excessive or stimulating food and drink; limit and renew possession of ground; avoid discussion, contemplation, and recollection concerning women; and do not occupy beds or couches affected by desire. Finally, they avoid love and hate in response to sounds.

l: the five great vows, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The five great vows concern abstaining from killing living beings, lying speech, taking what is not given, sexual pleasures, and attachments. Each has five clauses and must be practised according to the precept. Called a place of peace, great teachers, and producers of disinterestedness, they are proclaimed as light illuminating three worlds and repelling darkness.

l: the first great vow: abstinence from killing any living beings, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: renounces killing living beings [whether subtile or gross, movable or immovable] The first great vow renounces killing living beings, whether subtile or gross, movable or immovable, and forbids killing, causing killing, or consenting to killing. Its five clauses require careful walking, examination of the mind and speech, careful handling of begging utensils, and inspection of food and drink.

l: the second great vow, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: renounces lying speech [arising from anger, greed, fear, or mirth] The second great vow renounces lying speech arising from anger, greed, fear, or mirth, including speaking lies, causing others to speak lies, or consenting to them. Its five clauses require deliberation in speech and renunciation of anger, greed, fear, and mirth.

l: the third great vow, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: renounces taking anything not given [in a village, town, or wood; living or lifeless; little or much; small or great] The third great vow renounces taking anything not given, whether in a village, town, or wood, and whether living or lifeless. Its five clauses regulate begging, consumption with permission, limited and time-bound possession of ground, renewal of grants, and begging for co-religionists.

l: the fourth great vow, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: renounces sexual pleasures [with gods, men, or animals] The fourth great vow renounces all sexual pleasures with gods, men, or animals. Its five clauses prohibit continual discussion of women, contemplation of their forms, recollection of former pleasures with women, excessive or unsuitable eating and drinking, and occupying beds or couches affected by women, animals, or eunuchs.

l: the fifth great vow, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The fifth great vow renounces attachment to all things, whether living or lifeless, and forbids forming, causing, or consenting to attachment. It unfolds through five clauses requiring non-attachment to agreeable and disagreeable sounds, forms, smells, tastes, and touches.

l: Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Liberation, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The Sixteenth Lecture, Called the Liberation, concludes the Second Book by teaching wise mendicants to abandon attachments, endure suffering harmlessly, meditate on supreme truth, and attain freedom from pain.
proclaims supreme truth [as doctrine] The supreme truth is identified as the doctrine of the Tîrthakara, upon which one should meditate.
is_a doctrine [of the Tîrthakara] The supreme truth concerns the temporary residence of creatures in the four states of being. Hearing it, the wise should meditate upon it.

l: mendicant (the wise sage), Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: The mendicant is a matchless, great sage and good Sramana. Self-controlled, unattached, and free from desire, he leaves family bonds, acts, and attachments, collects alms, and lives among householders and monks. He endures words, blows, pain, and pleasure without harming any beings. Steadfast suffering increases his austerity, wisdom, and glory; with conquered sensuality he meditates on virtue, walks in wisdom and restraint, and is freed from former sins and the bed of pain.

l: wisdom and restraint, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Wisdom and restraint govern the mendicant's life and walk. A mendicant who is constant, bears pain, and walks in wisdom and restraint loses the dirt of formerly committed sins.

is_a boundless flood of water [difficult to traverse with the arms alone] Samsâra is compared to a great ocean, a boundless flood of water difficult to traverse with the arms alone. The learned one should know and renounce it.

l: Maker of the end, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: Maker of the end is a sage who knows and renounces samsâra, understands bondage and deliverance according to doctrine, has quitted the path of births, and as a monk has neither support nor standing place.

l: bondage and deliverance, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: are_declared amongst men Bondage and deliverance are declared among men and in the doctrine. The sage who knows them according to that doctrine is called 'Maker of the end.'

l: path of births, Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra)
s: is_quitted_by Maker of the end [when there is no bondage in this world or the two other continents] The sage for whom there is no bondage in this world, or in the two other continents, or in heaven and hell, has quitted the path of births.
ends Second Book [after the Sixteenth Lecture] The unit marks the end of the Âkârâṅga Sûtra.

This document summarizes the first book of the Sutrakritanga, a sequence of sixteen lectures on bondage through Karman and liberation through disciplined religious life. Sudharman, Gambûsvâmin, Mahâvîra, Rishabha, Kêvalin, Kâsyapa, Arhat Gñâtriputra, and the Venerable One frame or convey its teachings. Its central claim is that possessions, violence, passions, false doctrine, sensual attachment, and carelessness bind the Soul to Karman, repeated birth, death, suffering, and hells; restraint, non-killing, purity, detachment, austerity, meditation, truthful conduct, and control of mind, speech, and body lead toward Nirvâna, Môksha, Peace, and final Liberation. The work first rejects views denying rebirth, moral causation, the Soul, or the true Law, then teaches that every being bears the consequences of its own Karman and that worldly ties are transient. It addresses the trials of monks, hostility, hunger, weather, injury, insult, illness, relatives, rulers, heretics, and desire, and urges endurance, mutual care, and adherence to the Law. Several lectures warn especially against sexual temptation, domestic attachment, property, and harmful conduct; the description of hells illustrates the torments awaiting sinners. Mahâvîra, also called Gñâtriputra and Vardhamâna, is praised as the omniscient teacher who conquered passions, annihilated Karman, and proclaimed the highest Law. The later lectures define careful monastic conduct: avoid injury, theft, sexual intercourse, false speech, improper food, attachment, and alms linked to slaughter; obey wise teachers; accept correction; and treat all beings tenderly. They criticize false creeds and merely external practices, affirming that right knowledge and right conduct, not ritual alone, free one from the Circle of Births. The book closes by describing the qualities of the true Brâhmana, Sramana, Bhikshu, and Nirgrantha: one who abandons sin and passion, subdues the senses, endures hardship, follows prescribed conduct, and seeks Liberation.

is_a book [translated work] It presents teachings on the bondage of Soul, the causes of Karman and misery, and the conduct leading toward Nirvâna. It records discussions of Mahâvîra’s doctrine and criticisms of competing philosophical views.

Mahâvîra is a Gina, Arhat, Sramana, Nirgrantha, great sage, and famous native of Vaisâlî, also called Gñâtriputra and Vardhamâna. He possesses highest and infinite knowledge and faith, infinite perception, omniscience, virtue, and freedom from impurity, passion, greed, and all ties. Homeless and renouncing everything, he practises control, contemplation, abstinence from women and night eating, and austerities; he keeps nothing, bears everything, and grants protection to all. He understands every philosophical system and knows this world and that beyond. By conquering wrath, pride, deceit, and greed, committing no wrong, and annihilating all Karman, he reaches insurpassable perfection. He teaches, puts forward, and proclaims the highest Law of the Ginas and sacred texts. His doctrine presents possession, violence, and attachment as causes of bondage and misery, teaches innumerable births, and makes non-killing the legitimate conclusion of wisdom. In his concluding teaching, monks are urged to avoid killing, abstain from sins, and seek spiritual welfare. He is praised as the flag and best of monks, the best teacher of Nirvâna, the wisest sage and man, and without an equal.

Sramanas are religious ascetics, not monks who seek houses with fine food. They may hold true or heretical doctrines; those who deny the true Law, pursue pleasures, or abuse the pure path enter a wrong path. Heretical Sramanas are ignorant and careless, incur sin, misery, destruction, and great danger, and remain subject to Karman, death, and repeated birth.

Brâhmanas are religious practitioners and Kriyâvâdins who perform customary acts and dispute truth. Some explain the world through Brahman or a primeval egg, while others deny true words or the Law and suffer misery. They understand the world according to their lights and teach that right knowledge and conduct lead to liberation.
A heretical creed with doctrines among varied opinions: it teaches three ways of sin, misery from one’s works, and liberation through right knowledge, conduct, and understanding.
is_a heretical creed It is named as one of the four heretical creeds.

Soul is an unchangeable entity that appears as the world in various forms and is bound by possessions, violence, passions, and wrong conduct. Though some say it ends after death or deny rebirth, the teaching says it experiences pleasure and pain and may become free from Karman. Its benefit, liberation, is sought through truth, restraint, austerities, Guptis, detachment, and subduing the senses; abandoning possessions delivers it from misery.

Karman is an evil force and the accumulated consequence of actions. It increases through killing, causing or approving killing, greed, pride, deceit, wrath, impure thought, violence, carelessness, passions, and sinful acts; it is not acquired when new acts are avoided. It impels wrongdoing even when its consequences are known, causes suffering through the fruit of works, determines punishment when bad Karman ripens in hell, and keeps beings in the Circle of Births and Samsâra. It has six sources, though the Akriyâvâdins deny it. The wise understand its influx and stoppage. Karman is removed through renunciation that knows the value of life, and annihilated through control, austerities, detachment, penance, restraint, purity, and abstention from sinful actions. A monk who controls actions and senses, avoids violence, and suppresses Karman and will can destroy bad Karman. Mahâvîra annihilated all his Karman through knowledge, virtue, faith, and austerity. The Great Hero without Karman is neither born again nor dies.

l: bondage of Soul, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: Bondage of Soul is caused by possessions, ownership, attachment, violence, sinful activity, and passions; knowing and removing these causes enables escape from misery.

Nirvâna is the chief object of the Law and a state consisting in peace. It is reached through purity of heart, restraint, and freedom from Karman, especially by ceasing to injure living beings. It is also associated with abstaining from false speech, refusing what is not freely given, carefulness, and pursuing real good. Heretical doctrines and careless conduct do not lead to it. Mahâvîra, praised as Gñâtriputra, is presented as the best among those who taught Nirvâna.

Samsâra is the Circle of Births: a long, impassable, boundless flood or stream in which beings undergo repeated birth, death, disease, old age, pains, and new Karman. Wrong doctrines, sinful conduct, attachment, and seduction by the senses and women keep beings within it and lead to repeated rebirth and danger. It carries along those who remain mixed with the world and prevents them from reaching the opposite shore. Practitioners seek escape by resisting seductions, ceasing from works, annihilating Karman, renouncing everything, and following the true Law and the Path. Mahâvîra and monks cross this difficult flood through knowledge, carefulness, and resistance to seductions; the true Law ends it.

The Law is the highest, pure, complete, and unparalleled doctrine of the Ginas, Kêvalins, Kâsyapa, Mahâvîra, and Arhats. Associated with knowledge, self-control, restraint, and freedom from Karman, it is taught, argued, demonstrated, pondered, searched for, and made manifest by those who have learned and considered it. Its central demands are non-injury to living beings, truthfulness, restraint from taking what is not freely given, freedom from sexual pleasure and property, renunciation, detachment, austerities, careful conduct, proper speech, subduing the senses, and guarding against transgression in words and thoughts. It distinguishes sin, rejects false doctrine and individual falsification, and should be taught truthfully, clearly, without blameable practices, passion, or a wish to please or irritate. By following it, practitioners cease actions, destroy Karman, stop the current of Samsâra, cross misery and transmigration, and move toward peace, Liberation, or the end of mundane existence. Those who ignore or do not know it do not attain these ends and are beyond right faith; those who learn, consider, and reveal it are to be honoured.

l: the five gross elements, Sutrakritanga (Sûtrakritâṅga), Book I
s: The five gross elements are earth, water, fire, wind, and air; some philosophers claim they produce Soul and other things, but the text presents this claim as mistaken doctrine.

The world contains living and lifeless, movable and immovable beings experiencing varied pleasure and pain. Philosophers dispute whether it is created, eternal, limited, or boundless; it is also called unreal in a quoted view. The text refutes creation doctrines, describes it as eternal, says it will not perish, and says awakened men know its past, present, and future ways.
The body is abandoned by the person who subdues the senses and is well qualified for the task.

Misery arises from sin, wicked deeds, possessions, violence, passions, and wrong understanding. It is produced by one’s own works: living beings suffer the consequences of their deeds and cannot escape them before experiencing them. Its forms include hardships such as cold, hunger, insults, blows, temptation, attachment, and the continuous bodily and mental pain of the hells. Those who do not know its origin cannot know its prevention, and false or wrong paths lead to misery and destruction. The wise understand its influx and annihilation, endure suffering patiently without passions, and follow restraint, right knowledge, and the Path toward liberation from all misery.

Sin is a wicked deed that causes misery, suffering, further births, and punishment in the hells. It may be committed through one’s own activity, commission, or approval of another’s deed; sinful thoughts reveal an impure, careless mind. Attachment contributes to sin, which includes killing or injuring beings, false speech, taking what is not freely given, sexual pleasure, owning property, and failing to practise control. A sinner may conceal or deny conduct when reprimanded, committing further sin for reputation. Bad deeds lead to corresponding severe punishments. The teachings require abandoning sin, especially killing, and call on a corrected monk to promise not to repeat it, distinguish sin, and annihilate it through proper conduct.

Death is an event that affects all living beings, including young and old people and children in the mother’s womb. It repeatedly overtakes beings caught in wrong doctrines, passions, and Karman; when life is spent, none can prolong it, and each goes and comes alone. Every high or low, movable or immovable being ultimately leaves the body and dies. Death is ended by the true Law.

Birth continues without number for beings in Samsâra following wrong doctrines, taking many existences and repeatedly being born after harming living beings. Human birth is difficult to obtain; men may die at any stage. Birth ends through true knowledge, restraint, and the true Law.

Beatitude is the highest good and final goal, also called liberation or perfection. It is reached through religious life, disciplined conduct, restraint, a pure soul, renunciation of fetters, destruction of Karman, and enduring hardships while wandering. A monk pursues it by overcoming pleasures, passions, greed, and attachment, following the Law and rules of conduct until crossing Samsâra. It is not obtained through possession, worldly undertakings, uncontrolled conduct, bathing, contact with water, or tending fire; claims that such practices liberate are refuted. Presented as the best thing, like the moon among the stars, Beatitude is brought about by a restrained sage who subdues the senses and is reached by those who avoid approval or disapproval of disputed gifts.
Property is a possession monks should abandon: sought for liberation or clung to by men, it brings harm and increases iniquity, especially through deadly pleasure-seeking acts.

Non-killing is the quintessence of wisdom and reciprocity’s legitimate conclusion. Because beings are subject to pain, it requires ceasing to injure or kill every living being, as presented first in the doctrine and again on the path.

addresses sons (Rishabha's sons) [as a teacher] Rishabha tells his sons to acquire perfect knowledge of the Law, cease from sin, control themselves, and follow the path leading to the destruction of Karman. He teaches that all beings individually suffer for their own deeds and that human birth is difficult to obtain again.

Kâsyapa is an illustrious, omniscient religious teacher associated with and proclaiming a Law practiced through abstinence, control, hardship, and care for sick brothers. This Law is followed by virtuous Ginas of past and future. Kâsyapa warns that attachment is a dangerous whirlpool avoided by the wise but entered by the ignorant, describes hellish pains and punishments to Kêvalin, and proclaims the very difficult Path by which a monk crosses the dreadful current of Samsâra toward the supreme condition.
Gñâtrika is a great seer who knows everything in the whole world and proclaims the Law of right conduct and spiritual welfare, whose followers become virtuous, righteous, and mutually confirm it.

Living beings are all forms of life and existence described as earth, water, fire, wind, plants, grass, trees, corn, animals, and creatures that move or do not move. They suffer and experience pleasure and pain according to their own Karman, owe their present existence to it, and remain subject to birth, old age, death, and repeated rebirth. All desire happiness, hate pain, and will meet death. Yet people harm them through killing, injury, cutting, dismembering, and sciences or spells intended for destruction, often for comfort, pleasure, or amusement. The lectures repeatedly direct wise people and monks to stop such harm: no being should be killed or injured, directly or through others, by hand or foot, in thought, word, or act. Restraint and tender treatment toward every class of being, wherever it is found, are presented as protection of the soul and as part of the peace called Nirvâna.

Heretics seek truth without crossing Samsâra, yet unworthy members entertain false doctrines, oppose the Law, and become slaves of women. Some rely on gods to end misery; they revile monks and defend worldly and sexual pleasures through assertions and abuse.
